Preterition
pret-uh-RISH-uhn
doctrinal phrase
From Latin praeteritio, a passing by, from praeterire, to pass over; the passing-by of the non-elect in the decree of reprobation.

📖 Biblical Definition

Preterition is the theological term for the first part of the decree of reprobation—God’s sovereign passing by of those whom He has not chosen unto salvation, leaving them in the fallen and sinful condition into which all mankind fell in Adam. Reformed theology distinguishes two elements in reprobation: preterition, the negative act by which God in His sovereign good pleasure passes over the non-elect and does not give them the saving grace bestowed on the elect; and condemnation, the positive act by which He justly ordains them to punishment for their sins. The distinction guards a vital truth: God’s passing by is according to His unsearchable will and not according to any foreseen worse sin in the reprobate than in the elect, for all alike were fallen and deserving of wrath; but the condemnation of the reprobate is always just, grounded in their own real sin, so that God is in no way the author of their sin nor unjust in their punishment. The elect are saved by sovereign grace they did not deserve; the reprobate perish by a justice they did deserve. The dictionary holds preterition as the necessary counterpart of election: if God from eternity chose some unto salvation, He thereby passed by the rest, for the choice of some out of a fallen mass is the not-choosing of others. The doctrine humbles the saved, who can claim no merit, and silences every charge of injustice against God, who owes salvation to none and wrongs none in leaving the guilty to the just reward of their sin. The mystery of preterition is to be received with reverence, not pried into with presumption.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The sovereign passing-by of the non-elect in the decree of reprobation—God leaving them in their fallen state—distinguished from the just condemnation grounded in their own sin.

PRETERITION, God’s sovereign passing by of the non-elect.

The negative element of reprobation, distinguished from positive condemnation.

God passes over the non-elect according to His unsearchable will, not foreseen worse sin.

Their condemnation is just, grounded in their own real sin.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Preterition is either denied outright or distorted into making God the author of sin, against the careful balance Scripture requires.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the careful Reformed distinction between preterition and condemnation, which guards God’s justice and sovereignty together. God passes by the non-elect according to His sovereign good pleasure, not because of any foreseen worse sin in them; but He condemns them justly for their own real sin, so that He is in no way the author of their sin nor unjust in their punishment. The elect are saved by grace they did not earn; the reprobate perish by justice they did deserve.

The doctrine is corrupted in two ways. Some deny preterition altogether, recoiling from the hard truth and so denying the sovereignty of God in election, as if His choice of some did not entail the passing by of others. Others distort it, speaking as if God were the author of the reprobate’s sin or condemned men apart from their guilt, a slander Scripture forbids—God tempts no man and condemns none unjustly. The dictionary holds the reverent balance: preterition is sovereign and according to God’s will; condemnation is just and according to men’s sin. The mystery humbles the saved and silences the creature’s charge against the Creator, and it is to be received with worship, not pried into with presumption.

The term names the passing-by of the non-elect, the negative side of reprobation, held with God’s perfect justice.
